stories.title: n8n Website Data Extraction to JSON
stories.summary: An n8n and OpenAI workflow discovers website datasets, processes Excel, CSV and HTML tables, and prepares structured JSON with schemas and tags.

image.caption: Illustrative overview of website dataset discovery, format-specific processing and the JSON handoff.

gallery.caption: Project data processor canvas, showing the separate Excel, CSV and HTML table paths.

gallery.alt: Excel workbook extraction and conversion to JSON
gallery.caption: Project Excel-to-JSON subworkflow for turning spreadsheet content into structured data.

gallery.alt: Table normalization, schema generation and tagging workflow
gallery.caption: Project table-to-JSON transformer, including schema generation and tag extraction.

gallery.alt: Error classification and structured logging workflow
gallery.caption: Project error-handler subworkflow for recording processing failures in a structured log.

gallery.caption: Project fatal-error notification workflow, kept separate from routine error logging.

gallery.caption: Project main orchestration canvas connecting source discovery, subworkflows and JSON output. These editor captures show the workflow structure, rather than a measured completeness or accuracy result.

children.value: Website datasets were spread across downloadable spreadsheets, CSV files and HTML tables. The task was to start from supplied URLs, discover relevant data sources and organize their contents for downstream analysis instead of handling each format separately.
n8n orchestration with an OpenAI discovery agent to find candidate dataset links from starting URLs.
Separate processing paths for Excel, CSV and HTML tables, with reusable table-to-JSON subworkflows.
Schema generation and classification, including geographic and subcategory tags.
JSON output organized by starting URL, containing dataset entries and a processing log.
Configurable crawl settings and URL-pattern filtering for the requested language scope. The language filter checks URL patterns rather than translating or verifying every page's language.
Structured error logging and a separate notification path for fatal failures.

The workflow connects discovery and format-specific processing to a common JSON handoff. Schemas, tags and logs provide context for downstream tools and for investigating failures. New website structures and unusual file formats can require processor changes.
Who this approach suits
Teams collecting recurring website datasets for analysis or internal tools. To scope similar work, bring starting URLs, example source files, required fields and the intended JSON format.
Discuss website data extraction

stories.title: Invoice Photo OCR to Excel with Python
stories.summary: A local Python OCR tool extracts client names, addresses and tax IDs from a known invoice-photo layout, with the source filename retained in each Excel row.

image.alt: Invoice photos pass through a fixed client-region crop and layout-specific OCR parsing into Excel rows with source filenames.
image.caption: Invoice photos pass through a fixed client-region crop and layout-specific OCR parsing into Excel rows with source filenames.

gallery.alt: Illustrative OCR workflow from invoice input through recognition and field parsing to structured data.
gallery.caption: Concept illustration supplied for the gallery. The 94% faster wording and JSON/database endpoint shown here are not delivered results; this project reads invoice photos and exports client fields to Excel.

gallery.alt: Spreadsheet output with source filenames and extracted client fields
gallery.caption: Project spreadsheet example showing the source filename and client-field columns. It is not presented as the output of the separate invoice image in this gallery or as an accuracy evaluation.

gallery.alt: Invoice image with bounding boxes showing extracted client information via OCR.
gallery.caption: Project OCR demonstration with boxes over the client block. The numbers beside the text are OCR recognition scores for this image, not measured field accuracy; seller details elsewhere on the invoice were not extracted by the delivered parser.

children.value: The task was to move client details from a batch of invoice photos into a spreadsheet. The supplied layout placed those details in a consistent region, allowing the tool to focus on the client block rather than parse the whole invoice.
A local Python batch script reads files from an invoice folder.
OpenCV crops a fixed region on the right side of each photo before PaddleOCR recognizes the text.
A layout-specific parser extracts the client name, address and tax ID.
pandas writes Excel columns for source_file, client_name, client_address and tax_id, keeping the original filename for checking the source photo.
Unreadable files, empty OCR results and processing errors are logged and skipped.

The delivered tool provides a local photo-to-Excel handoff for client fields in the supplied layout. Extracted values still need review: the parser uses layout rules rather than validating invoice accuracy. Seller fields and different invoice layouts require additional work.
Who this approach suits
Teams collecting client details from repeatable invoice-photo layouts into Excel. To scope a similar tool, bring redacted photos, the fields required and an example of the desired spreadsheet.
Discuss invoice photo extraction

stories.title: n8n Invoice Extraction with Validation and Review
stories.summary: An n8n invoice workflow extracts headers and line items, translates descriptions, checks totals, and sends reviewable data to Google Sheets for an Excel handoff.

image.caption: Illustrative n8n invoice workflow from intake through extraction, translation and checks into human review and spreadsheet output.

gallery.alt: Illustrative invoice verification workflow with extraction, validation, comparison and error flags.
gallery.caption: Concept illustration supplied for the gallery. Purchase-order matching, Azure OpenAI and the accuracy or audit-ready wording shown here are not claims about this project's delivered workflow.

gallery.alt: Original M2 invoice orchestration workflow
gallery.caption: Earlier invoice orchestrator canvas, showing intake, extraction and spreadsheet handoffs. The 97.9% annotation is an internal target, not a verified project accuracy result.

gallery.caption: Project error-notification workflow, showing the log, failed-file handling and email notification path.

children.value: Invoice processing involved more than copying totals. The workflow needed to retain original descriptions, add English translations, and fit an existing spreadsheet review process without overwriting formula columns.
The task was to connect PDF and image intake to structured invoice data, while making questionable documents, duplicate records and extraction failures visible to a reviewer.
Google Drive intake and n8n orchestration for individual PDF and image invoices.
AI extraction of invoice headers and line items, retaining Greek descriptions alongside English translations.
Document classification, VAT and total checks, with success, review, duplicate and failed states. Duplicate candidates remain available for human acceptance or rejection.
Correction memory from records marked Active or Corrected. It can reuse supplier details and line descriptions while preserving raw audit values and formula columns.
Google Sheets output designed for the existing Excel and Power Query handoff, plus failure logging and notifications.

The delivered core connects intake, extraction, checks and reviewable spreadsheet output. Review states and retained source values give finance staff a way to investigate an invoice before accepting it. The combined multi-invoice PDF extension remained work in progress.
Who this approach suits

Finance and operations teams that need invoice extraction to fit their spreadsheet rules and approval process. To scope similar work, bring redacted invoices, required fields, document languages and the workbook structure.
Discuss an invoice automation workflow

stories.title: LangGraph Project Planning Assistant
stories.summary: A LangGraph assistant clarifies a project brief, researches subtasks and assembles a Markdown implementation plan for technical review.

image.alt: Illustrated AI project planning workflow from a goal through task breakdown and dependencies to an action plan.
image.caption: Conceptual overview of a LangGraph planning assistant. A project brief passes through clarification, research and report generation before technical review.

gallery.alt: Clarification, supervisor, research and report-generation agent graph
gallery.caption: Architecture of the public planning implementation. Inspect clarification, supervised research, research compression and the report-generation and tool-review stages. This graph shows implementation structure, not a completed client run.

gallery.alt: Fictional Markdown planning example with a CSV-import goal, three steps, their dependencies and a technical-review requirement.
gallery.caption: Fictional Markdown plan for a CSV-import task. The goal, steps and dependencies illustrate the handoff format; this image is not a captured agent result or a verified estimate.

children.value: A short project idea can leave important requirements unstated. The goal was to turn that brief into a structured plan a developer could inspect, rather than hide assumptions inside one long AI answer.
A clarification stage that asks follow-up questions when the brief is incomplete.
A supervisor that assigns research topics to specialist research agents.
Research-tool execution and a compression stage that summarizes findings for the supervisor.
A report-generation stage that combines the research brief and findings into a structured Markdown plan.
A human-review step for protected file-tool calls.
Modular Python code, model and research configuration, tests, and a repository example plan.
Inputs and handoff

The input is a project description, refined through clarification. The report prompt organizes the plan around technology choices, features, architecture and implementation phases. Configuration controls the research tools, models and iteration limits. The public repository includes an example Markdown plan; the gallery's short CSV-import plan is a separate fictional illustration.

The implementation makes the path from requirements to research and a plan inspectable. A developer can use the draft to discuss scope and dependencies before implementation. Technical review remains necessary for the proposed design, estimates and assumptions.
Who this helps
Product and engineering teams exploring an assistant for preparing project plans. This work illustrates capabilities relevant to an
AI Workflow Buildout
For a similar project, share a short brief, the plan format you need and the decisions that should stay with your team.

A spreadsheet queue for search inputs.
A browser workflow that searches using those inputs and returns result links.
Write-back fields for result URL, timestamp and row status.
Configurable concurrency for parallel search tasks.

The worksheet holds the search inputs and receives result links and execution status. Operators can inspect individual rows and open the returned links. The handoff includes a parallel-run entry point and environment instructions; a returned URL is not evidence that a booking was completed.

stories.title: Webcam Distance Estimation with Depth Anything V2
stories.summary: A Python computer vision prototype combines object detection and depth estimation to display approximate distances between detected objects in a webcam view.

image.alt: Webcam path combining RT-DETR and Depth Anything V2 into a distance overlay. The stored reference scale and assumed camera geometry require setup-specific validation.

children.value: Object boxes show where something appears in an image, but do not tell an application how far away it is. This project explored combining object detection with monocular depth estimation in a repeatable webcam prototype.
A Python webcam loop combining RT-DETR object detection with Depth Anything V2.
Filtering for the configured person and cup classes, with per-object distance labels in feet.
Spatial calculations and a distance line when exactly two objects are detected.
Project settings and an environment lockfile for repeatable setup.

The diagram follows the running webcam path. A separate navigation module exists in the source but is not called by that loop. Distance conversion uses a stored reference scale and assumed camera geometry; it is not a validated measurement system.
The prototype makes estimated spatial relationships visible in a webcam overlay, giving a product team a concrete starting point for camera-specific experiments.
Where this fits

stories.title: Color-Coded Schedule PDF Extraction to Excel
stories.summary: A Python extractor turns staff schedule PDF grids into Excel rows, preserving dates, shifts and color-coded request values for coordinator review.

image.alt: Native-PDF schedule extraction into Excel. Fictional calendar entries use the implemented numeric request legend: 0 Off, 1 Available, 2 Request to Work.
image.caption: Illustrative native-PDF schedule extraction into Excel. Fictional calendar entries use the implemented numeric request legend: 0 Off, 1 Available, 2 Request to Work.

gallery.alt: Original schedule PDF extractor implementation
gallery.caption: Implementation screenshot showing schedule-key filtering, continuation-page handling and the Excel export call.

gallery.alt: Fictional schedule rows using the implemented request-code legend. This is an example of the Excel handoff, not a client workbook or accuracy result.
gallery.caption: Fictional schedule rows using the implemented request-code legend. This is an example of the Excel handoff, not a client workbook or accuracy result.

children.value: Staff schedule PDFs encode preferences through both their calendar layout and highlight colors. Copying the text alone loses that meaning, and a person's schedule can continue across pages.
The task was to convert native PDF calendars into spreadsheet rows for scheduling review. The documents were staff schedules rather than clinical records.
Python and PyMuPDF read the PDF text and drawing objects, then detect the calendar grid. This path requires native PDF content rather than scanned photos.
Schedule-key pages are skipped, and continuation pages remain associated with the current person.
Each extracted row carries NAME, Date, Year, WEEKDAY, SHIFT and REQUEST. Repeated date, shift and request entries within the extraction pass are filtered out.
The request legend is 0 = Off for yellow or pink; 1 = Available for no highlight or near-white; and 2 = Request to Work for green.
Cells without a readable date and highlights outside the recognized color rules are skipped. Excel output includes the request-code legend.

The result is a schedule-to-Excel extractor that keeps dates, shifts and preference codes together for a coordinator to review. Its grid and color rules are specific to the supplied PDF format, so a different calendar layout or legend needs adaptation.
Who this approach suits
Scheduling teams moving recurring calendar PDFs into spreadsheets. To assess a similar workflow, bring a redacted native PDF, its color legend and the columns your team needs.
Discuss schedule PDF extraction

stories.title: n8n Record Sync and a PostgreSQL Query Assistant
stories.summary: n8n workflows separate record create, update and delete operations, alongside a schema-aware PostgreSQL chat assistant.

image.alt: Record synchronization and a separate SQL query assistant. SELECT text checks and a default LIMIT 100 do not guarantee read-only database access or a maximum result size.
image.caption: Illustrative record synchronization and a separate SQL query assistant. SELECT text checks and a default LIMIT 100 do not guarantee read-only database access or a maximum result size.

gallery.alt: Fictional SELECT query and two example rows. The schema and values illustrate the handoff, not an executed agent result.
gallery.caption: Fictional SELECT query and two example rows. The schema and values illustrate the handoff, not an executed agent result.

children.value: The team needed scripted data flows expressed as inspectable n8n workflows, plus a separate way for operators to ask questions of PostgreSQL. Record synchronization had to keep create, update and delete behavior distinct. Database questions needed their own schema and query-tool path.
This case brings together two related pieces of automation work:
n8n workflows for collecting, comparing, enriching and synchronizing records.
Separate create, update and delete routes, with vector-index updates in the synchronization flow.
Confidence thresholds that branch enrichment and creation decisions.
A shared error workflow attached to collection, comparison, lookup and create operations. The inspected update and delete exports do not attach that error workflow.
A PostgreSQL chat assistant that retrieves schema information and calls an SQL executor tool.
Query-validation code intended to check SELECT statements and disallowed keywords, with a fallback LIMIT 100 when the query text contains no LIMIT.
Inputs and handoff

The synchronization workflows operate on source records and their downstream destinations. The assistant uses database schema information to prepare queries. Its text checks do not establish database-enforced read-only access or a maximum row count; database permissions and query controls need validation before operational use.
The synchronization routes make record changes and enrichment decisions easier to inspect. The separate assistant demonstrates schema-aware database question answering.
Who this helps
Operations teams maintaining synchronized records or exploring database question answering. An
AI Workflow Buildout
can scope the data handoff, review rules and operational controls together.
For a similar project, share the source and destination systems, the synchronization rules and examples of approved database questions.

Reusable commands for local, unified and pull-request linting workflows.
Linter execution and processing of its results.
AI-assisted review-text generation from code-quality findings.
Repository helpers for branch, commit, pull-request and comment operations.
Modular workflow configuration, tests and usage documentation.

The toolkit works with repository changes and code-quality results. It prepares linting output and assisted review text, with helpers for agreed repository operations. It is a Python automation toolkit used around existing CI and repository tools, rather than a replacement hosting platform.

The handoff makes workflow decisions available as reusable Python components instead of leaving all orchestration inside workflow YAML. Engineers can inspect the workflow modules and review the AI-assisted drafts before using them in their quality process.

Engineering teams needing maintainable automation around repository quality checks. Discuss a defined integration through an

stories.title: Resumable Python Listing Extraction to CSV
stories.summary: A Python listing extractor saves results incrementally to CSV and JSON Lines, then uses completed listing IDs to resume interrupted batches.

image.alt: Listing extraction with incremental CSV and JSON Lines output. Restart reads completed listing IDs from saved JSON Lines records; processing settings are defined in code.
image.caption: Illustrative listing extraction with incremental CSV and JSON Lines output. Restart reads completed listing IDs from saved JSON Lines records; processing settings are defined in code.

gallery.alt: Fictional listing_id and url values illustrate CSV and JSON Lines records. Resume reads listing IDs from saved JSON Lines, rather than a separate checkpoint file. This is not a client export or measured run.
gallery.caption: Fictional listing_id and url values illustrate CSV and JSON Lines records. Resume reads listing IDs from saved JSON Lines, rather than a separate checkpoint file. This is not a client export or measured run.

children.value: The client needed structured data from many listing pages. Restarting an interrupted batch should not mean repeating every completed listing, and reviewers needed usable output before the final page had finished.
Separate stages for collecting listing URLs and extracting their details.
Concurrent workers with request delays and retry handling.
Incremental CSV and JSON Lines output as records complete.
Resume logic that reads listing IDs already saved in the JSON Lines file and skips them on a later run.
Progress reporting and optional environment-based proxy settings.
Inputs and handoff

The extractor starts from source listing pages and saves detail records to files for review. Worker count, delays and retry limits are set in the scraper code; they are not user-facing runtime controls. The saved JSON Lines records provide the completed-ID store rather than a separate checkpoint file.

The result is a batch-extraction process with visible progress and output that can be reused across interrupted runs. Incremental files let reviewers inspect completed records while the batch continues. Changes to page layouts and source access still need maintenance and validation.
Who this helps
Teams collecting listing data through a defined, authorized process. A
Data Extraction Automation Sprint
can scope the fields, source access and export handoff.
For a similar project, share a sample listing URL, the fields you need and your preferred output format.

stories.title: Football Player Tracking with YOLO and Team Colors
stories.summary: A Python football-video pipeline combines YOLO detection, jersey-based team colors and ByteTrack IDs to produce annotated match footage for visual analysis.

image.alt: Football pipeline combining YOLO detection, appearance-based team grouping and tracking IDs into annotated match video.
image.caption: Illustrative football pipeline combining YOLO detection, appearance-based team grouping and tracking IDs into annotated match video.

gallery.alt: Football match demonstration with team-colored player markers, tracking IDs and a ball marker.
gallery.caption: Thirty-second demonstration from the football repository, re-encoded for the website. Team-colored ellipses and tracking IDs overlay a recorded match. The poster comes from this clip; playback frame rate is not a processing-speed result.

gallery.alt: Football detector validation F1-confidence curves for ball, goalkeeper, player and referee classes.
gallery.caption: Detector validation F1 versus confidence on the 49-image validation split. The all-class curve peaks at 0.90 at confidence 0.359; the ball curve is weaker. This chart measures detection, not tracking accuracy.

gallery.alt: Football detector confusion matrix with raw class counts and background rows and columns for missed and unmatched detections.
gallery.caption: Raw detector validation counts for ball, goalkeeper, player and referee. The background row represents missed detections; the background column represents unmatched predictions. It is not a fifth trained class.

children.value: Turning recorded football footage into a useful visual-analysis baseline requires more than detecting people. Players need team labels and tracking IDs, while goalkeepers, referees and the small ball need distinct detection classes. This project connects those components in one configurable video-processing pipeline.
YOLO detector training for four classes: ball, goalkeeper, player and referee, using a public Roboflow football dataset.
Jersey-based team grouping that adapts Roboflow's team-classification approach, using pretrained SigLIP embeddings, UMAP and two-cluster KMeans.
ByteTrack IDs through Ultralytics tracking, with an alternative BoT-SORT configuration.
Team-colored player ellipses, tracking labels and a triangle marker when the ball is detected.
Hydra configuration for model, tracker and annotation settings, with annotated video output.
The diagram shows the implemented path from recorded video to the overlay. The gallery clip demonstrates team colors and IDs, while the two charts describe detector validation.
Published detector validation

The repository reports a YOLOv12L result on 49 validation images containing 1,174 labeled objects: precision 0.948, recall 0.880, mAP50 0.916 and mAP50-95 0.675. Player mAP50 is 0.994; ball recall is 0.618, making the ball the weaker class. These are published box-detection results, not measurements of tracking identity consistency, team assignment or processing speed. The evaluation was not rerun for this case study.

The implementation turns a match recording into an annotated video that can be inspected with team colors and tracking IDs. The public clip and validation plots make the result concrete, while the weaker ball detection identifies a useful target for further model work.
View the public football tracking implementation
Where this fits
